quote: Macroscopic decoherence—also known as “many-worlds”—is the idea that the known quantum laws that govern microscopic events simply govern at all levels without alteration.
content: This identification is the sequence’s central move and it is a conflation. Decoherence is a physical process, the suppression of interference between components of a system’s state through entanglement with its environment; it is accepted, and used, by every interpretation, including collapse theories and pilot-wave theory, and it is a matter of calculation, not interpretation. Many-worlds is the further claim that the decohered components are each a world containing observers, that nothing else happens, and that the squared amplitudes are the probabilities those observers should expect. The standard review of decoherence says plainly that “decoherence does not solve the measurement problem” and that its use to support Everett requires additional interpretive commitments (Schlosshauer (2005)); Opus’s annotation on Many Worlds, One Best Guess quotes the field to the same effect. By writing “decoherence (a.k.a. many-worlds)” throughout, the sequence lets every experimental confirmation of decoherence (which are many) count as confirmation of many-worlds (which they are not), and lets the question “do you accept decoherence?” stand in for “do you accept that there are other worlds?” Every physicist accepts the first. The essays that follow, Decoherence Is Simple and Decoherence Is Falsifiable and Testable, are titled for the process and argue for the interpretation.

quote: Read literally, this implies that knowledge itself—or even conscious awareness— causes the collapse. Which was in fact the form of the theory put forth by Werner Heisenberg!
content: Heisenberg held nearly the reverse. His view was that the wavefunction represents in part the observer’s knowledge, that the “reduction” is a change in that knowledge rather than a physical process, and that the cut between quantum system and classical apparatus can be placed anywhere (Physics and Philosophy, 1958, ch. III: the discontinuous change “is a consequence of the fact that our knowledge changes”); that is the epistemic reading that Quantum Non-Realism will attack under the name of “Goofus,” not consciousness-causes-collapse. The consciousness view belongs to von Neumann’s chain as read by London and Bauer (1939) and to Wigner (“Remarks on the Mind–Body Question,” 1961), who later abandoned it. The essay’s history of collapse theories runs: first knowledge, then, out of nervousness, objective collapse. The actual sequence was: von Neumann’s projection postulate (1932), Bohm’s deterministic alternative (1952), Everett (1957), Wigner’s consciousness proposal (1961), and the dynamical collapse models of Ghirardi, Rimini and Weber (1986) as an explicit physical mechanism. Objective collapse was not a retreat from dualism; it was a response to the vagueness of “measurement,” and it came after Everett.

quote: The only phenomenon in all of physics that is non-local in spacetime and propagates an influence faster than light.
content: Several items in this list are wrong about the collapse theories that exist, as opposed to the textbook postulate. Dynamical collapse models (Ghirardi, Rimini & Weber (1986); continuous spontaneous localization; the review by Bassi et al. (2013)) are precisely specified, continuous (CSL is a stochastic differential equation, not a discontinuity), and satisfy no-signalling: nothing propagates faster than light in the sense of transmitting information, and relativistic versions with Lorentz-invariant statistics exist (Tumulka (2006); Bedingham et al. (2014)). What Bell’s theorem forces on any single-outcome theory is nonlocality of correlations, which is not the same as superluminal influence, and it forces it equally on pilot-wave theory, which the sequence never mentions. “Non-linear,” “non-unitary” and “stochastic” are true of collapse models and are what makes them testable, since they predict deviations from unitary quantum mechanics (spontaneous heating, X-ray emission, loss of interference above a mass scale) that experiments are now constraining (Donadi et al. (2021)). That is the answer to “does any collapse theory have any experimental support?”: no, and the experiments that could give it are being run and are excluding parameter space, which is what a live theory looks like. The list is a catalogue of aesthetic complaints against an unspecified postulate, offered as physics.

quote: Yet collapse theories considered in modern academia only postulate one surviving world. Why?
content: Because a collapse theory that left many worlds would be Everett with a superfluous mechanism. The better question, which the sequence never asks, is why its menu has only two items. The pilot-wave theory of de Broglie (1927) and Bohm (1952) is single-world, deterministic, realist, has no collapse, no observer-dependence and no vagueness about measurement, reproduces every prediction of quantum mechanics, and is the theory Bell recommended as the one that should be in the textbooks (Bell (1982)). It is nonlocal, as Bell’s theorem requires of any single-world theory, and it has its own problems (a preferred foliation for the relativistic version; the status of the quantum equilibrium hypothesis). Every one of the eight sins on this essay’s list, except nonlocality, is absent from it. The fourteen essays of this sequence contain no mention of it. A reader who finishes the sequence believes that the alternatives to many-worlds are an informal textbook postulate and a mysticism about consciousness, and that belief is the product of an omission, not an argument.
